q.intro.text: Elm Street and Oak Street are parallel. A rail line crosses both. Where it meets Oak Street, one corner is sixty-five degrees. What is corner x, where it meets Elm Street? Pick an answer, and say how sure you are.

e.intro.text: Four steps. Press each one. The figure moves first, then the notation.

e.step0.text: Two crossings, P and Q. The band between the parallel streets is the interior. The sixty-five degree corner and x are both inside it, on the same side of the rail line.

e.step1.text: Slide Oak Street's crossing up the rail line until Q lands on P. The streets are parallel, so it lands exactly on Elm Street. The sixty-five degree corner lands on corner y. So y is sixty-five degrees. They are corresponding angles.

e.step2.text: x and y together fill a straight line: the rail line, one hundred eighty degrees. So x is one hundred eighty minus sixty-five, which is one hundred fifteen degrees.

e.step3.text: One hundred fifteen plus sixty-five is one hundred eighty. Same-side interior angles at parallel lines add to one hundred eighty degrees. They are not equal.

e.why.text: Quick check: why could the sixty-five degree corner move up to Elm Street?

e.why.ok.text: Yes. Parallel is what makes the slide land exactly. Without it, the corners would not match.

e.why.look.text: Looks can fool you, and a drawing may not be to scale. The reason is the slide, which needs parallel streets.

e.why.equal.text: They are not equal: one hundred fifteen and sixty-five. Same-side interior corners add to one hundred eighty degrees.

t.intro.text: Now the parallel lines l and m stand up, and the given angle is one hundred eight degrees. The first step is done for you.

t.partner.text: Which marked angle is the alternate interior partner of the one hundred eight degree angle?

t.p.ok.text: Yes. Angle a is between the lines, on the other side of t. Watch the half turn about M carry the one hundred eight degree angle onto a.

t.p.b.text: Angle b is between the lines too, but on the same side of t. That makes it same-side interior. Alternate means opposite sides.

t.p.c.text: Angle c is outside the lines. It corresponds to the one hundred eight degree angle. Alternate interior angles are both between the lines.

t.a.text: What is the measure of angle a?

t.a.72.text: The half turn put the one hundred eight degree angle right on top of a. Alternate interior angles are equal, not supplementary.

t.a.no.text: The half turn carried the one hundred eight degree angle exactly onto a. So what is a?

t.a.ok.text: Yes. Angle a is one hundred eight degrees. Alternate interior angles at parallel lines are equal.

t.b.text: Angle b is on the same side of t as the one hundred eight degree angle, between the lines. What is its measure?

t.b.108.text: Angles b and a sit side by side on line m. Together they make a straight line. They add to one hundred eighty degrees, so b is not one hundred eight.

t.b.no.text: Angles a and b fill a straight line together. They add to one hundred eighty degrees.

t.b.ok.text: Yes. Angle b is one hundred eighty minus one hundred eight, which is seventy-two degrees. Angle b and the one hundred eight degree angle are same-side interior angles: they add to one hundred eighty.

q.cb.right.text: At the start you picked one hundred fifteen degrees, and you were right. Now you can show why: slide, then use the straight line.

q.cb.equal.text: At the start you picked sixty-five degrees. Corners between the lines on the same side are not equal. They add to one hundred eighty degrees.

q.cb.cant.text: At the start you picked can't tell. With the streets given as parallel, you can tell: the slide lands exactly.

q.cb.none.text: Parallel lines let you move an angle from one crossing to the other. Then a straight line does the rest.

p.intro.text: Riley added the angles of five triangles. The sums were one hundred eighty, one seventy-nine, one eighty-one, one eighty, and one eighty. So every triangle makes one hundred eighty. Is that a proof?

p.test.text: Five examples are not a proof. It must work for every triangle. Line l is drawn through A, parallel to B C. Pick each reason.

p.build.text: Right. Examples are not a proof. Line l is drawn through A, parallel to B C. Pick each reason.

p.no.look.text: Looking parallel is not enough. Line l was drawn parallel to B C. That is the reason.

p.no.circ.text: That is exactly what we are trying to prove. It can't be a reason in its own proof.

p.no.other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line. Which reason makes this line true?

p.c1.text: Right. A half turn about the middle of A B carries angle B onto angle one.

p.c2.text: Right. A half turn about the middle of A C carries angle C onto angle three.

p.c3.text: Right. Angle one, angle A and angle three fill line l. That is one hundred eighty degrees.

p.c4.text: Right. Watch A slide. The argument never used a size.

p.done.text: That's a proof. Every claim has a known reason, and it works for every triangle. Riley's triangles were only examples.
